stories.title: China just had a 12-day coding-model fire-sale
stories.why_you_care: Top-tier AI coding just got 3× cheaper — and it didn't come from the usual suspects.
stories.body: In a twelve-day window in mid-May, four Chinese labs — Z.ai (GLM-5.1), MiniMax (M2.7), Moonshot (Kimi K2.6), and DeepSeek (V4) — released open-weights coding models that match the agentic-engineering (AI doing the actual coding work, not just suggesting lines) ceiling of frontier closed models, at roughly one third of the inference cost. Quietly. In twelve days.
stories.more: The frontier isn't moving up anymore — it's moving down on price. When open models hit the same capability ceiling at a third of the cost, "which model is smartest?" gives way to a sharper question: where does the money go when intelligence is cheap? Expect inference-cost wars, more coding agents shipping inside products you already use, and a fresh round of build-vs-buy conversations at every enterprise.

stories.title: Gemini quietly stopped being a chatbot
stories.why_you_care: Google is shifting Gemini from "another AI app" to "the AI that's already inside everything you use."
stories.body: At Google I/O on May 19, Google announced Gemini 4.0 plus three companions: Gemini Omni (a video model whose outputs are grounded in real knowledge), Gemini Spark (a personal agent that runs tasks across Workspace, Search, Chrome, and YouTube), and Gemini 3.5 Flash hitting GA (generally available — meaning anyone can use it now) at roughly 4× the speed of comparable models.
stories.more: The shift isn't any single new model — it's that Gemini is being repositioned from a destination app to an OS-layer running quietly across Google's surfaces. The chatbot-vs-chatbot framing already feels dated. The new question is which AI quietly lives inside the tools you reach for every day, without your noticing.

stories.title: AI just had its first real security moment
stories.why_you_care: The same models writing your code are now finding bugs in everyone else's — and there are 5× more of them than usual.
stories.body: Palo Alto Networks' May Patch Wednesday (the monthly day when security teams disclose what they fixed) disclosed 26 CVEs — over five times their typical monthly volume — and the majority were surfaced by frontier AI models scanning code, not human researchers.
stories.more: This is the crossover month: AI's contribution to defensive security stopped being a future story and became a production reality. The uncomfortable flip side is that the same class of models is presumably finding the same bugs for attackers. Expect a year of vulnerability-triage catch-up, faster patch cycles, and awkward conversations about responsible-disclosure norms.

quick_hits.text: of car sensor data — NVIDIA dropped open data on a scale nobody else has matched: Alpamayo (autonomous-vehicle models), Nemotron (agentic AI), plus 10T language tokens, 500K robotics trajectories, and 455K protein structures.
Raindrop's Workshop — an open-source local debugger for AI agents — shipped for Mac, Linux, and Windows with a one-line install. The first credible one, by most accounts.
Japan Airlines made humanoid robots permanent staff at Haneda — a three-year operational commitment from a regulator-cautious legacy airline, not a press conference.
— Anthropic announced a joint venture with Blackstone, Hellman & Friedman, and Goldman Sachs to push AI into community banks and regional health systems. The API-only era is ending.

quick_hits.lede: Even Meta is renting compute now.
quick_hits.text: It signed a multi-billion-dollar deal to rent Google's TPUs and raised its 2026 AI capex guidance to $125–145 billion. The most cash-rich company in the field is leasing chips from a rival.

fun_fact.title: A robot just hit elite-human level at table tennis.
fun_fact.body: Sony AI's "Ace" is the first known autonomous system to compete with professional-level humans in a popular physical sport — quietly clearing a benchmark researchers have circled for two decades. The wild part: it learned mostly from self-play.
